result.summary: A collection of short fragments attributed to Hesiod, quoted by later writers. They touch on Linus the singer, Apollo and Paean, the power of the king of the gods, nymphs and Satyrs, gifts of gods to heroic families, and proverbs about conduct.

scenes.title: Quoted fragments of lost verse
scenes.summary: Unconnected quotations from lost poems, preserved by ancient authors and scholars. They mix myth, genealogy, ritual and proverbial wisdom.

alias_notes.explanation: Hesiod came from Boeotia, so Bacchylides calls him the Boeotian.
Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: A memorable proverb warning against abandoning what one has for what one lacks.
Bacchylides' quotation of Hesiod on divine favour and good repute.

analysis.text: The fragments share concerns typical of Hesiodic poetry: the gods' gifts, proper ritual, and practical wisdom.
These lines survive only as quotations by later writers such as Strabo, Clement and scholiasts, showing how much early Greek epic is lost.

fun_facts.text: Several fragments are known only because scholars quoted them to explain a word or a line of Homer.

language_notes.text: Linus was a legendary musician whose death was mourned in the 'Linus song', a lament sung at feasts and dances. Urania is the Muse of astronomy.
Paean is the divine healer of the gods, here named as a figure of healing; the name later became an epithet of Apollo.
Curetes were divine youths who danced in armour; in some stories they guarded the infant Zeus. Satyrs were rustic woodland spirits, here scorned as worthless.
The sons of Aeacus (such as Peleus and Telamon) were famed for strength, those of Amythaon (such as Melampus) for seercraft, the Atreidae for wealth.
Spits are the metal skewers on which meat was roasted over a fire.
Dodona was the oldest Greek oracle, where Zeus spoke through the rustling of oak trees. The Pelasgi were an ancient pre-Greek people.
'The Boeotian' means Hesiod, who came from Boeotia in central Greece. 'Followeth' is archaic for 'follows'.

context_notes.text: These fragments are quotations preserved by later writers such as Diogenes Laertius, so the original poems and their order are lost.
The 'king and lord of all the undying gods' is most likely Zeus, ruler of the Olympian gods.
The Parthenius was a river in Paphlagonia, on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor. Its name is related to the Greek word for maiden.

literary_notes.text: Three balanced clauses assign a different gift to each family, giving the line a neat, memorable structure.
The river's gentle flow is compared to a delicate girl's walk, and the comparison echoes the river's name, Parthenius.
The line gives compact folk wisdom, warning against abandoning what one has to chase what one lacks.
